paragraphs.en: The [[fortnightly]] ferry to Grey Harbour smelled of diesel and wet rope, and I stood at the rail with the other [[passengers|passenger]], watching the [[island]] rise out of the morning mist.
I had left the [[south-western]] coast [[recently]] enough that the place still felt familiar, yet I felt no [[nostalgia]] for it, only a mild [[wonder]] at how small it was.
Five years in the city had made the town feel [[tiny]]; the same [[grey]] water, the same roofs, the same [[unmistakable]] smell of salt.
My [[great-grandmother|great-grandparent]] would turn ninety on Sunday, and every branch of the [[household]] was coming home for it.
A [[fellow]] biologist from the [[workstation]] waved from the pier, and I [[greeted|greet]] him with a [[tight]] hug before we walked up the [[main]] street.
Her [[house]] had not changed: the low ceiling, the [[fireplace]] with last night's [[fire]] still breathing, the same smell of wood smoke.
She sat in an [[upholstered]] chair that was older than I was and [[comfortable]] in a way no new furniture is.
The only [[adornment]] on the wall was a faded photograph of the mine, and the [[centrepiece]] of the room was a table she had polished for sixty years.
At ninety her [[age]] was written in her hands, but her [[blood]] still ran warm and quick, and a faint [[tint]] of rouge sat on her cheeks.
She studied my face as if reading a [[list]] of everything I had failed to write to her about.
After tea she opened an album and pointed to a girl in a [[miniskirt]] standing beside a [[horse]], one hand on the [[reins|rein]].
That girl was my mother, and the [[bole]] of the tree behind her had been cut down the year the [[mine]] closed.
In the next photograph a [[group]] of men stood at the pit head, and no one could [[deny]] that the work had broken their backs.
Great-grandfather had [[toiled|toil]] in the [[shaft]] for thirty years, and a single [[collapse]] had taken eleven men.
She spoke of [[childbirth]] too, of her own mother dying young, and then she [[ceased|cease]] and looked out of the window.
[[Five|five]] names were [[depicted|depict]] in the margin, and she had watched each of their children [[grow]].
At the harbour the [[fish]] market was already busy, and the smell of [[boiling|boil]] crab shells hung over the [[flagstones|flagstone]].
The old fishermen said the bay had been [[overfished|overfish]] for a decade, and each season the [[finite]] catch grew smaller.
A [[hound]] [[chased|chase]] a [[chick]] across the road, and a young man in rubber [[boots|boot]] pulled it back by the collar.
They [[served|serve]] hot soup from a [[booth]] near the quay, and I ate standing up, [[chewing|chew]] slowly while the wind [[thrust]] my hair into my eyes.
A [[linguist]] from the university was recording the old dialect, and she said the word for [[shedder]] crab would die with my grandmother's generation.
Nobody mentioned the plant, but the word passed from mouth to mouth like a [[warning]], and the [[ground]] under our feet felt less solid than it looked.
My own [[workstation]] in the city was stacked with [[data]] on fish [[tissue]], and I had come home with a simple [[mission]]: to measure how fast the bay could recover.
Our [[dean]] had signed the [[fee]] agreement, and the [[ethical]] review had taken a year.
The [[chemical]] plant upstream had been [[overfunded|overfund]] by a [[misguided]] grant, and its celebrated [[breakthrough]] existed mostly on paper.
I had [[first-hand]] evidence that the water was cleaning itself, and that seemed a small [[miracle]].
[[Hopefully]] the council would listen to a [[local]] scientist rather than to a [[diplomat|diplomacy]] from the capital.
Back in the lab, the [[inefficiency]] of the old [[workplace]] was obvious, and we spent a week [[disassembling|disassemble]] a [[conveyor]] built for [[oversize]] crates.
Only then would the [[basic]] samples [[fit]] on the bench.
On Monday I walked to the [[dentist]] because a filling had come loose on the ferry, and the chair was as [[uncomfortable]] as I remembered.
The light above my [[nose]] was too bright to let me [[check]] my watch, and he gave me a [[liquid]] to rinse with.
He told me not to [[chew]] on that side for a day and gave me a [[tip]]: [[over-the-counter]] painkillers were enough.
It was [[unnecessary]] to [[tire]] myself with worry, he said, and [[sadly]] he was [[partly]] right.
That evening the town hall was full because the [[mayor]] had called a meeting about the plant.
A [[poll]] in the local paper said the town was split, and the [[agenda]] on every seat was printed in red.
A [[lobbyist|lobby]] for the company, a smooth [[executive]] in a grey suit, tried to [[persuade]] us that the plant was safe.
He was visibly [[hostile]] to questions, and his answers were full of [[misinformation]] and [[groundless]] claims.
The [[minister]] from the regional government [[denied|deny]] that any [[indirect]] [[link]] existed between the plant and the dead fish.
The [[chief]] engineer was the only [[person]] on the panel willing [[to]] answer questions directly.
An old miner rose and said that the first [[boom]] had lasted fifteen years, and that the river had begun to [[perish]] after the first spill.
He was [[aghast]] that the company wanted to [[overstep]] the [[boundary]] of the old industrial [[zone]].
Beyond it lay the marsh, a [[border]] between land and water where [[worms|worm]] and young fish hid.
If the plant [[polluted|pollute]] that nursery, the whole bay would suffer, for some fish change [[sex]] as they mature and need calm water to reach [[sexual]] maturity.
For years the old workings had lain [[dormant]], and the company's [[founder]] had promised to leave them alone; the promise now looked like a form of [[guardianship]] nobody had asked for.
Silence [[reigned|reign]] after he sat down.
At home my great-grandmother listened to the radio report and said nothing for a long time.
Then she told me about the winter of the flood, when a visiting preacher had delivered a [[sermon]] on patience and the town had lost its boats anyway.
She said her husband had been a man of few [[words|word]] who [[embodied|embody]] [[adherence]] to a promise.
What [[horrified|horrify]] her was not the storm but the way officials spoke about it afterwards.
Her [[diplomacy]] at the dinner table had kept a divided family [[together]] for fifty years.
I wanted to [[cheer]] her, but she only [[shook|shake]] her head and smiled.
On the day of the vote the [[flag]] above the school hung at half-mast for a fisherman lost at sea.
People queued across the flagstones to the booth, and the queue itself was [[strikingly]] quiet.
The result was not [[unanimous]], but the plant was [[rejected|reject]] by a clear majority.
The square became [[lively]]; each [[individual]] had a face I half knew, and the [[huge]] crowd seemed [[unstoppable]] for a minute.
The fight was not only about fish; it was about a [[workforce]] that had been [[marginalized]] for a generation.
Tourism and [[retail]] had replaced the old [[industry]], and the [[inequality]] between summer visitors and winter residents was plain.
Fishermen could not [[insure]] their boats for a season without a loan, and it was [[unrealistic]] to ask them to wait.
The company had tried to [[cheat]] the town with a [[baseless]] survey, and its figures [[overlapped|overlap]] suspiciously with the ones it had published before.
Any deal would [[entail]] a [[setback]] for the company, and the town should not [[discriminate]] between small boats and large ones.
A small [[boost]] to the harbour budget might [[settle]] more than a grand plan.
The company's report was [[unreliable]] and largely [[untested]], and its [[title]] promised more than the data showed.
A common [[misconception]] was that the sea could absorb anything; the [[literal]] truth was that it could not.
We should not [[overrate]] a single [[slipup]], but we should not [[overlook]] a pattern either.
The survey was [[outdated]] and its authors [[inexperienced]], yet a crowd of [[unreflecting]] readers took it as gospel.
When the council [[announced|announce]] the rejection, the company threatened to sue, then quietly withdrew.
That night my aunt [[hosted|host]] a dinner of [[boiled|boil]] fish and [[green]] vegetables, and the table was loud with [[chatter]].
My cousin [[entertained|entertain]] us with stories of her first year as a teacher, and her [[enthusiasm]] was infectious.
My great-grandmother [[chatted|chat]] with the youngest [[child]] and let him [[grip]] her finger.
The [[recent]] argument was forgotten for an hour, and the [[bond]] between the generations felt stronger than any vote.
After dinner I sat in the [[shade]] of the porch and watched the lighthouse [[shine]] across the bay.
My phone buzzed: the new sensor data had arrived, and I opened the [[app]] to read it.
[[Unlike]] the old paper log, the screen showed every tide minute by minute, and a [[cue]] told me the sampler was still working.
[[Maybe]] the town could live with the sea rather than against it; [[furthermore]], it might even profit from doing so.
Then [[hail]] began to rattle on the roof, small and hard, and I thought of the [[minor]] repairs still undone.
The [[work]] of persuasion would go on [[worldwide]] and at home, and I wondered whether I had already [[outgrown|outgrow]] the town or only begun to see it.
On Tuesday I [[boarded|board]] the ferry again, and this time I did not [[miss]] the island as I had before.
The town would [[depend]] on the next council, and the council would depend on people who bothered to attend.
I could [[envisage]] a smaller plant, a cleaner river, and a school that taught children to fish with care.
[[Human]] beings are [[inescapably]] part of the ecosystem, not visitors to it.
As the boat [[entered|enter]] the channel, the [[world]] outside the bay seemed less urgent than the one I was leaving.
I would stay [[until]] the last of the summer, and then come back.
My great-grandmother [[agreed|agree]] to come to the city for the winter, on one condition: that I bring her back in spring.
It was a [[win-win]] arrangement, she said, and for once nobody laughed at the phrase.
The ferry pulled out, and the island shrank to a grey line.
I opened my notebook and wrote the first line of a report I finally understood.
